successors.name: Nabataean Kingdom
successors.text: Dedan and Tayma: Lihyan 'fell into the hands of the Nabataeans around 65 BC' (some authors), annexed 'around 24 BC' (Caskel), with Dedan reached 'in 9 BC'

ledger.x: 6th century BC (bridged): the kingdom of Dadan stands at the AlUla oasis.

c. 552 BC: Nabonidus conquers Dedan and Tayma. 'Nabonidus swept through northwestern Arabia in c. 552 BC; eliminating the kings of both Tayma and Dadan'; 'By March or April, Nabonidus had defeated the king of Dadanu, and had captured other cities in Arabia, including the city of Tayma, which he had…

c. 543 BC (bridged): the Lihyanite kingdom replaces the Dadanite. 'The Lihyanite kingdom most likely came into being after the arrival of Nabonidus in north-west Arabia in 552 BC'; Dedan 'served as the capital for two successive kingdoms'. Winnett has the Lihyanites 'appeared in the 4th century BC' and Rohmer and…

c. 24 BC: the Nabataeans annex Lihyan. 'The Nabataean annexation of Lihyan was around 24 BC' (Caskel); 'fell into the hands of the Nabataeans around 65 BC' (some authors); Aretas IV's inscription at Hegra is dated around 9 BC. Nabataean rule over Lihyan 'ended with the annexation of Nabatea by the Romans in 106 AD'.

c. 24 BC: the Lihyanite kingdom ends under the Nabataeans. The page's end for the kingdom itself is disputed: Winnett has it vanish in the 2nd century BC, Rohmer and Charloux in the mid-3rd century BC; the Nabataean annexation is the first date that is a political event.

wars.name: Nabonidus's Arabian campaign
wars.outcome: Nabonidus 'fighting against the king of Dadanu' by December 553 or January 552 BC, then defeating him and capturing Tayma by March or April 552; he rules from Tayma until 543/542 BC.

wars.name: Nabataean annexation of Lihyan
wars.outcome: Lihyan 'fell into the hands of the Nabataeans around 65 BC' (some authors), 'around 24 BC' (Caskel); the Nabataeans reached Dedan 'in 9 BC'.

certainty.note: The oases are named but no frontier; the kingdom's dates are disputed (Winnett against Rohmer and Charloux).
